newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: HORSE RACING-Oscar Schindler Melbourne Cup favourite.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-Oscar Schindler Melbourne Cup favourite.

text.p: MELBOURNE, Nov 4 - The owner of Melbourne Cup favourite Oscar Schindler on Monday said his camp felt confident, NZPA reports.
"I'm quietly confident, or nervously confident," Oliver Lehane said on the eve of Australasia's biggest race.
"His trainer and his work rider thinks the horse is in fantastic form."
Oscar Schindler has not raced since his slashing third in one of the world's most prestigious races, the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe in Paris on October 6.

That form has been made all the more significant with Arc runner-up Pilsudski going on to win one of the world's richest races, the $US4 million ($NZ5.70 million) Breeders' Cup Turf (2400m) in Canada last week.
At his previous start, Oscar Schindler won the group one Irish St Leger on September 21 which also has a Melbourne Cup significance.
The Irish St Leger was won by Vintage Crop both before and after becoming the first Northern Hemisphere-trained horse to win the Melbourne Cup in 1993.

Lehane, 53, who made his wealth from banking and slot machines and is now involved in nursing homes in Ireland, said Oscar Schindler's winning time of two minutes 59.1 seconds for the 2800m of the St Leger was notable.
"Vintage Crop won the St Leger twice and Oscar Schindler's time was seven and eight seconds faster."
Lehane said it would have been his preference for Oscar Schindler to have contested the Breeders' Cup Turf in Canada rather than the Melbourne Cup.
But trainer Kevin Prendergast, who was born in Melbourne but lived most of his life in Ireland, was able to twist Lehane's arm.
"My trainer always had the Melbourne Cup in mind for this horse, being born here.
"He wanted to come here hell or high water. And at the end of the day he had his way."
Lehane said it would have cost less to race the horse in Canada.

Oscar Schindler has certainly not been lonely while in quarantine at the Sandown race course in Melbourne. In addition to trainer Kevin Prendergast, also on hand have been his stable foreman, a personal vet and a strapper.
"If you want to do something, do it right," Lehane said.
"And I'm out here just to pay the bills."
Rival English trainers say the only chink in Oscar Schindler's armour may be his ability at the cup distance of 3200m.
Oscar Schindler has not raced beyond 2800m but Lehane said there was no doubt in Prendergast's mind about the horse's ability to tackle the longer distance.
"My trainer assures me it is not a problem."
Another in the cup from the Northern Hemisphere is Istidaad, but he has been in Australia since May.
He has raced five times in Australia and gained his first win last Saturday week in Melbourne when taking out the group two $A125,000 Moonee Valley Gold Cup (2500m).
Greg Hall, who won the Melbourne Cup in 1992 with Subzero, is the rider of Istidaad.
"He's had six months here, he's now acclimitised," Hall said.
"I think this horse will improve out of sight from the Moonee Valley Gold Cup.
"I liked the way he stuck his head out; he was a beaten horse half-way up the straight.
"He's going to have to find another five lengths but I think he will do that."
Istidaad is owned by Sheikh Hamdan Bin Rashid Al Maktoum of Dubai.
The sheikh has won two previous Melbourne Cups with At Talaq in 1986 and Jeune in 1994.
At Talaq was trained by Colin Hayes, Jeune by Hayes' son David and an elder son Peter is the trainer of Istidaad.
One of New Zealand's leading chances is The Bandette, trained by John Wheeler at New Plymouth.
Wheeler said The Bandette shaped as promising a stayer as Wellington Cup winner Flying Luskin.
Wheeler was not the trainer of Flying Luskin when he won the Wellington Cup, but was the horse's original trainer before complications for the owners led to the horse being sold.
"Flying Luskin was my first winner in Australia," said Wheeler, who has had about 50 winners.
The Bandette has raced only 16 times but showed he was stayer of high promise when at his 10th start finished second in the group one $A700,000 Sydney Cup (3200m) last April.
"I don't think there would have been many New Zealand horses that would have run in a group one race over two miles within their first dozen starts and run a place."
Wheeler said the only reservation about The Bandette was his lack of experience, but said the horse was now at the age where he needed to go into the deep end.
"He's a five-year-old so he's got to be able to cop a bit now.
"He's very close to the very best class."
Wheeler has two Melbourne Cup runners, the other being The Phantom Chance, who was trained in Auckland by Colin Jillings at Takanini when he won the $A1.5 million Cox Plate (2040m) in 1993.
The Phantom Chance was unplaced for Wheeler in last year's Melbourne Cup and gained his first win in the group two $175,000 weight-for-age O'Shea Stakes (2400m) at Eagle Farm, Brisbane, last June.

The Phantom Chance has had mixed form recently but recorded two encouraging efforts -- second in the $A100,000 Canberra Cup (2000m) with the top weight of 60kg in September and at his next start was a solid fourth in the group one $A500,000m Metropolitan (2600m) at Randwick in Sydney.
Second and third in the Metropolitan were Nothin' Leica Dane and Saintly, both racing tomorrow.
The Phantom Chance suffers from a respiratory complaint equivalent to asthma and is treated with a ventilator up to twice a day.
However it was not used within four days of a race to avoid the the possibility of breaking any regulations from a swab, Wheeler said.
"He's a rather difficult horse to keep right and you can't tell if he's right unless he's under pressure.
"But I'm pretty happy with him at this stage and if you took a line through the Metropolitan form he would be a hard horse to beat."
